question_text: A 72-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of severe, acute, right leg pain for 2 hours. The patient's symptoms started suddenly while he was doing household chores. He has no history of leg pain at rest or with exertion. Yesterday, he returned home after a 6-hour bus ride from his grandson's home. He has hypertension treated with ramipril. He appears uncomfortable. His temperature is 37.4°C (99.3°F), pulse is 105/min and irregular, and blood pressure is 146/92 mm Hg. The right lower extremity is cool and tender to touch. A photograph of the limb is shown. Femoral pulses are palpable bilaterally; popliteal and pedal pulses are decreased on the right side. Sensation to pinprick and light touch and muscle strength are decreased in the right lower extremity. Which of the following is most likely to confirm the underlying source of this patient's condition?

                    ### Question
                    A 72-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of severe, acute, right leg pain for 2 hours. The patient's symptoms started suddenly while he was doing household chores. He has no history of leg pain at rest or with exertion. Yesterday, he returned home after a 6-hour bus ride from his grandson's home. He has hypertension treated with ramipril. He appears uncomfortable. His temperature is 37.4°C (99.3°F), pulse is 105/min and irregular, and blood pressure is 146/92 mm Hg. The right lower extremity is cool and tender to touch. A photograph of the limb is shown. Femoral pulses are palpable bilaterally; popliteal and pedal pulses are decreased on the right side. Sensation to pinprick and light touch and muscle strength are decreased in the right lower extremity. Which of the following is most likely to confirm the underlying source of this patient's condition?

                    ### Options

opb. Doppler ultrasonography of the legs
opc. Biopsy of a superficial vein
opd. Digital subtraction angiography
ope. Manometry

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The patient's acute right leg pain, coolness, and decreased pulses suggest an arterial occlusion, likely due to an embolic event. The irregular pulse indicates possible atrial fibrillation, which is a common source of emboli. Echocardiography is the most appropriate test to confirm the cardiac source of emboli, as it can identify thrombi in the heart, particularly in the context of atrial fibrillation. Digital subtraction angiography is useful for visualizing arterial blockages but does not identify the source of emboli. Doppler ultrasonography is more relevant for detecting deep vein thrombosis, which is less likely given the presentation. Therefore, echocardiography is the best choice to confirm the underlying source of this patient's condition, supported by the evidence path linking atrial fibrillation to echocardiography for detecting cardiac thrombi.
